effect_mechanism: Buffers remove nitrogen from water moving through the riparian zone.
conditionality: Highly variable; wider buffers more consistent; subsurface removal depends on soils and groundwater flow paths.
justification: Mayer et al. (2007) J. Environ. Qual., meta-analysis of 89 buffers / 45 studies [source_id mayer_2007_n_removal_meta], PDF p.2: "buffers were effective at removing large proportions of the nitrogen from water flowing through riparian zones (mean % 6 1 standard error [SE]: 67.5 6 4.0, N 5 88; Table 1)."

effect_mechanism: Riparian vegetation shapes stream chemistry via uptake, organic matter supply, flow modification and soil stabilisation.
conditionality: 'Substantial influence' read as moderate (no number); the review stresses that managing water quality through vegetation remains uncertain.
justification: Dosskey et al. (2010) JAWRA, review [source_id dosskey_2010_cited], PDF p.1: "Through the collective action of many processes, vegeta- tion exerts substantial inﬂuence over the well-documented effect that riparian zones have on stream water qual- ity."

conditionality: Can saturate and become a pollutant source under high nutrient loads.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.1: "riparian buffer strips also mitigate diffuse pollution and provide inputs to freshwater systems."

effect_mechanism: Forested riparian zones reduce sediment inputs and stabilise banks.
justification: Osborne & Kovacic (1993) Freshwater Biol., review [source_id rvb_wq_restoration_lowrance_1993], PDF p.1: "In small to mid-size streams forested riparian zones can moderate temperatures, reduce sediment inputs, provide important sources of organic matter, and stabilize stream banks."

effect_mechanism: Deep-rooted species support banks and reduce bank erosion.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.3: "Deeper rooted species, however, can provide support to riverbanks therefore reducing bank erosion and improve soil permeability thus increasing infiltration rates"

effect_mechanism: Riparian woodland creates habitat and connectivity.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.5: "Riparian woodlands can have positive implications for terrestrial bio- diversity, creating habitat for woodland specialists and enhancing wood- land connectivity, moreover, trees provide shade and shelter, buffering climatic extremes"

effect_mechanism: Fast tree growth on moist, nutrient-rich riparian soils.
conditionality: 'Extremely effective' is the review's wording for wooded buffers; no rate given in this sentence.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.5: "wooded buffers can be extremely effective at carbon sequestration, particularly in the early stages of development"

effect_mechanism: Slower overland flow, more infiltration, temporary storage.
conditionality: Wooded buffers; depends on ground-level roughness.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.5: "Wooded buffers can contribute to natural flood management, slowing the flow of water from the land into receiving water bodies by increasing infiltration, reducing flow velocity and providing temporary water sto- rage (Dixon et al., 2015; Tabacchi et al., 2000)."

effect_mechanism: Shade and shelter reduce livestock temperature stress.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.5: "Planting trees and shrubs in buffer strips also provides livestock with shelter from adverse weather (e.g. sun, rain and wind), alleviating tem- perature stress, and further benefitting production and welfare (Broom et al., 2013; Maseyk et al., 2017; Renaudeau et al., 2012)."

effect_mechanism: Wider buffers take farmland out of production.
conditionality: Cost largest on highly productive land.
justification: Cole et al. (2020) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., review [source_id managing_buffer_strips_es_review_2020], PDF p.8: "Wider buffers, however, take more land out of production, negatively influencing food production, and are thus more costly to sustain, especially in highly productive agricultural land where the greatest benefits can be achieved."
